t: Minimum Number of Swaps to Make the Binary String Alternating — Mismatch Counting Against Both Templates
o:
**Understanding the problem**

We may swap any two characters of the binary string s (positions need not be adjacent) and want the minimum number of swaps to make s alternating — no two adjacent characters equal — or -1 if impossible.

**Walking through Example 1:** s = 111000. The only alternating shapes of length 6 are 101010 and 010101. Against 101010, s differs at indices 1 and 4 (two mismatches); since one swap exchanges a misplaced 1 with a misplaced 0 and repairs both positions at once, that shape costs 2 / 2 = 1 swap. The shape 010101 mismatches at four positions and would cost 2. Answer: 1, matching the sample where swapping positions 1 and 4 yields 101010.

**Example 2:** s = 010 is already alternating, so zero mismatches means zero swaps.

**Example 3:** s = 1110 has three 1s but one 0; any alternating string needs counts differing by at most 1, so it is impossible and we return -1.

**What the constraints imply:** with n <= 1000 even an O(n^2) scan is safe, but feasibility depends only on character counts and cost on one linear mismatch count, so an O(n) solution falls out naturally.
k: Feasibility is a pure counting condition: even n requires ones == zeros == n/2; odd n requires the majority character to appear exactly (n+1)/2 times and occupy both endpoints.
There are only two candidate targets — 0101... and 1010...; evaluate both feasible ones and keep the cheaper.
One arbitrary swap fixes two mismatches simultaneously (a misplaced 1 trades places with a misplaced 0), so the cost of reaching a target is its mismatch count divided by 2.

a.i: For each of the two possible alternating shapes, first verify the character counts allow it, then walk s once counting positions that disagree with the shape. Against a valid template the number of misplaced 1s always equals the number of misplaced 0s, so halving the mismatch count yields the exact number of swaps. Take the smaller value over feasible shapes, or report -1 when neither shape survives the count check.
s: Count ones; set zeros = n - ones. If abs(ones - zeros) > 1 return -1.
Determine feasible starting characters: for even n both 0 and 1 work; for odd n only the majority character works (it must appear (n+1)/2 times).
For each feasible start c, expected[i] = c when i is even and the flipped bit otherwise; count differing positions m.
The cost for that template is m / 2; answer with the minimum over templates.
a.t: O(n) — one counting pass plus at most two linear scans over the string.
a.sp: O(1) — only counters and a walking expectation character.

a.i: Skip materializing templates entirely. In the pattern with 1s on even indices (starting 1010...), every 1 sitting at an odd index is misplaced, and because each swap relocates exactly one misplaced 1 together with one misplaced 0, the whole cost equals the number of such ones. Symmetrically, the pattern starting 0101... costs the number of ones at even indices. Feasibility filtering stays identical: equal counts admit both patterns, odd lengths force the majority character onto its required parity.
s: Count ones and zeros; return -1 if their difference exceeds 1.
Tally onesAtOdd = number of indices i where s[i] = 1 and i is odd; derive onesAtEven = ones - onesAtOdd.
If n is even, answer min(onesAtEven, onesAtOdd).
If n is odd, answer onesAtOdd when ones form the majority (they belong on even indices) and onesAtEven otherwise.
a.t: O(n) — two constant-work passes over the string.
a.sp: O(1) — a handful of integer counters.

w: State the impossibility condition first (counts differing by more than 1), then present Approach 2 — interviewers like that it never builds the templates. Pitfalls: this problem allows arbitrary-position swaps, unlike adjacent-only swap problems where you would count inversions instead; for odd lengths remember the majority character must take BOTH endpoints, so only one template is legal and comparing against the other silently produces wrong costs; do not forget that each swap fixes two positions, which is why no factor-of-2 confusion should survive testing. Edge cases: length-1 strings already alternate (answer 0), and all-equal strings longer than 1 are impossible except when n = 1. Likely follow-ups: minimum adjacent swaps to alternate (count inversions toward the nearer target), or making two different binary strings equal with minimum swaps.
